subtitle: ADX measures trend STRENGTH — telling you whether to trade trending strategies or range strategies. Stochastic finds extremes WITHIN trends — finding pullback entries when RSI shows nothing useful. Two underrated indicators that together fill important gaps.

blocks.content:
Two indicators that don't get the limelight RSI and MACD do but solve specific problems those don't. ADX answers "is the market actually trending?" — separating trend-following setups from range setups. Stochastic catches extremes within a trend that RSI misses because it's regime-saturated.

Both are worth understanding even if you don't use them daily — they fill blind spots in your other indicators.
ADX (Average Directional Index) is a non-directional momentum indicator. It only measures STRENGTH of the prevailing trend, not direction. Output is 0-100:

rows: Don't use trend-following setups; mean-reversion may work
Wait for confirmation before trend trades
Stay with the trend; don't fade strength
Watch for exhaustion; reversal more likely

blocks.title: The 25 threshold
blocks.content:
The most useful single number from ADX: ADX above 25 = trending market. Use trend-following strategies (BoS, pullback entries, riding the band).

ADX below 20 = ranging market. Switch to mean-reversion strategies (buy support, sell resistance, classic RSI 30/70).

Between 20-25 is transitional — wait for clarity. The trader who matches strategy to ADX regime avoids the most common mistake: trading trend strategies in ranges (lots of fakeouts) or range strategies in trends (constantly stopped out).

ADX comes with two companion lines that DO show direction:

  • +DI (positive directional index): measures bullish pressure
  • -DI (negative directional index): measures bearish pressure

When +DI > -DI = uptrend. When -DI > +DI = downtrend. The wider the gap, the stronger the directional bias.

Practical: ADX above 25 + +DI well above -DI = strong uptrend. ADX above 25 + -DI well above +DI = strong downtrend. ADX above 25 + DI lines close together = strong trend with mixed signals (rare).
Using ADX as a regime filter
ADX's best use isn't as an entry signal — it's as a FILTER for which strategy to apply:

rows: Trend-following: BoS pullbacks, momentum continuation, ride MAs
Mean-reversion: BB bands, classic RSI 30/70, range S/R
Trend-following (will get faked out in chop)
Wait — let the regime declare itself before committing

blocks.content:
The Stochastic Oscillator measures where current price closed relative to its recent high-low RANGE. Outputs %K (fast line) and %D (signal line, smoothed %K) — both 0-100.

  • Stochastic at 100 = price closed at the recent range's high (very strong relative position)
  • Stochastic at 0 = price closed at the recent range's low (very weak relative position)
  • Stochastic > 80 = "overbought" relative to recent range
  • Stochastic < 20 = "oversold" relative to recent range

blocks.title: Stochastic finds pullback extremes RSI misses
blocks.content:
In a strong uptrend, RSI camps at 70-80. "Pullback to 30" never happens — RSI never drops that far. But STOCHASTIC, which uses a short lookback (default 14 candles), catches each pullback within the trend. Stochastic of 20 within an uptrend marks a buyable pullback that RSI alone wouldn't reveal.

This is why stochastic and RSI together cover different territory. Use both for trending markets.

rows: Price has pulled back to the bottom of its recent range
Pullback entry zone — combine with support level + reversal candle
Momentum turning back up after oversold dip
Strong momentum continuing — normal trend behavior
Don't fade — stay in the trend
Higher highs in price + lower highs in stochastic
Warning of trend exhaustion (combine with other signals)

blocks.content:
Patterns that cost money:

  1. Ignoring ADX entirely. Trading the same strategy in trending and ranging markets = bleeding in one of them. ADX tells you which.
  2. Treating Stochastic 80/20 like RSI 70/30 universally. Stochastic is more sensitive (default 14 lookback). The 80/20 levels are touched more often. In strong trends Stochastic stays at extremes for long periods — same regime-classification rule applies.
  3. Using +DI/-DI as entry triggers. They lag like other crossovers. Useful as direction confirmation when ADX is above 25, not as entry signals on their own.
  4. Ignoring Stochastic in trending markets because "trends ignore overbought". Trends ignore SUSTAINED stochastic 80+, yes. But pullbacks to stochastic 20 within those trends ARE meaningful — the indicator's short lookback resets each pullback.
  5. Looking at ADX value without checking trend direction. ADX 40 tells you trend is strong; +DI vs -DI tells you which direction. Need both.

BTC 4H chart. Indicators show:

  • ADX = 32 (strong trend confirmed)
  • +DI = 28, -DI = 14 (well-separated, strong bullish bias)
  • Price in clear uptrend, just had a pullback to the 50 EMA
  • Stochastic dropped to 18 (oversold for this lookback)
  • RSI at 47 (mid-range — no signal alone but consistent with bullish regime pullback)
  • Pullback candle = bullish engulfing on above-average volume

This is a textbook A+ trend continuation setup:

  • ADX confirms trending market → trend strategies apply ✓
  • +DI confirms uptrend direction ✓
  • Stochastic caught the pullback that RSI missed ✓
  • 50 EMA as dynamic support ✓
  • Reversal candle + volume = entry trigger ✓

Trade:

  • Entry: Limit BUY at engulfing close + small buffer
  • SL: Below the 50 EMA and the engulfing candle's low
  • TP1: Recent swing high
  • TP2: Next major resistance

blocks.title: Take this with you
blocks.content:
Three rules:

  1. Use ADX as a regime filter. Above 25 = trending (trend strategies). Below 20 = ranging (mean-reversion strategies).
  2. Stochastic catches pullbacks in trends. What RSI camps over (70+ in uptrend), Stochastic resets each pullback to under 20.
  3. Combine indicators. No single one tells the full story. ADX + Stoch + RSI give you trend strength + pullback timing + momentum context.
